summary.text: A microbiome is the community of microorganisms that usually live together in a given habitat.
Researchers generally count bacteria, archaea, fungi, algae and small protists as members, while including viruses, phages and plasmids is more controversial.
Only a small proportion of microbes are linked to disease, most are essential for healthy ecosystems, and a healthy microbiome is essential for human health.

paragraphs.heading: A community, not a single microbe
paragraphs.text: A microbiome is the community of tiny living things that usually share one particular habitat. The living members of that community, taken together, are called the microbiota. Most researchers agree that bacteria, archaea, fungi, algae and small protists all count as members. Whether viruses, phages, plasmids and other mobile genetic elements belong is still argued over.

paragraphs.heading: Pinning down the word
paragraphs.text: In 1988 Whipps and colleagues offered a sharper definition: a typical microbial community living in a fairly well-bounded habitat with its own physical and chemical character. On this view the word covers not just the microbes but also the setting where they act, which Whipps called their theatre of activity. In 2020 an international panel of experts revived that definition. They added notes stressing that a microbiome is dynamic and drawing a clear line between microbiota and microbiome.

paragraphs.heading: How microbes talk to each other
paragraphs.text: Part of that theatre is chemistry. Secondary metabolites are chemicals that help different species deal with one another and survive amid competition. Through quorum sensing, bacteria use small molecules to coordinate shared work and adjust to the living things around them, which can lead them to stick together or build a biofilm. Over time it became clear that microbes do not live as lone cells but in complex groups where interaction and communication are critical.

paragraphs.heading: Every plant and animal has one
paragraphs.text: All animals and plants live alongside microorganisms, including protists, bacteria, archaea, fungi and viruses. Plants carry diverse microbial groups both inside their tissues, called the endosphere, and on their outer surfaces, called the episphere. These partners matter for plant ecology and physiology, for plant health and for food production. In mammals, the gut microbiome is now seen as a key regulator of the body, and hosts and microbes evolving together helped mammals adapt to many ways of life.

paragraphs.heading: Life in the sea
paragraphs.text: In the ocean, scientists long studied animals paired with just one symbiont. Newer work looks at how a marine animal interacts with its whole many-member microbiome. If microbiomes shape the health, behaviour and ecology of sea creatures, that could change how we think they cope with change. This matters most for the climate-related and human-caused changes already reaching the ocean and its phytoplankton microbiome.

paragraphs.heading: From animalcules to germs
paragraphs.text: Microbiome research grew out of microbiology, which began in the seventeenth century. The first microscopes opened up a hidden world and let people identify microorganisms. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek examined bacteria, fungi and protozoa, which he called animalcules, taken mostly from water, mud and dental plaque. He also found biofilms, an early hint that microbes interact in complex communities. Robert Koch explained human and animal diseases as the result of microbial infection, which turned attention to microbes as enemies to be wiped out.

paragraphs.heading: A new picture of microbes
paragraphs.text: The discovery of DNA, along with sequencing, PCR and cloning, let scientists study microbial communities without first growing them. Since the start of this century, new sequencing tools and the genetic data gathered with them have shown that microbial communities live everywhere on and in larger organisms. They have also shown how critical microbes are to the health of humans, animals and plants. Only a small share of microbes are tied to disease, while the great majority are essential to working ecosystems. For people, keeping the microbiome in good shape is essential to health, and it may become a target for new treatments.
